t.3.74.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Having seen every change in the wise Puṇyaśloka, Keśinī came back quickly and reported it all to Damayantī.
t.3.74.2: Then Damayantī, afflicted with sorrow and eager in her suspicion that it was Nala, once more sent Keśinī to her mother's presence.
t.3.74.3: Bāhuka has been tested by me many times on the suspicion that he is Nala; my one remaining doubt concerns his appearance, and I wish to find out for myself.
t.3.74.5: Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, the queen spoke to Bhīma, and the king gave his consent to that wish of his daughter.
t.3.74.4: Mother, either let him be brought in here, or you should permit me to go to him; whether my father knows of it or not, let this be arranged.
t.3.74.6: Then she, permitted by her father and by her mother, O bull of the Bharatas, had Nala brought into the place where her own quarters were.
t.3.74.7: But when she saw Nala in that condition, Damayantī, the lady of lovely complexion, was overcome with intense grief.
t.3.74.8: Then, O great king, Damayantī, clad in ochre garments, her hair matted, and smeared with dirt and grime, spoke these words to Bāhuka.
t.3.74.9: O Bāhuka, have you ever before seen any man, one who supposedly knows dharma, who abandoned a sleeping woman in the forest and went away?
t.3.74.10: Who but Nala of holy fame would go away, abandoning his blameless, beloved wife in a desolate place while she lay overcome by weariness?
t.3.74.11: What wrong have I done to that lord of the earth, who abandoned me in the forest and went away while I was overcome by sleep?
t.3.74.12: He whom I once chose, passing over the gods themselves in their very presence, how could he abandon me, his devoted and loving wife, the mother of his children?
t.3.74.13: Having taken her hand before the fire, her who stood by the words of the swans, and having truly promised, 'I shall cherish and support her,' where has that promise gone?
t.3.74.14: But as Damayantī was saying all this, O tamer of foes, abundant tears born of grief flowed painfully from her eyes.
t.3.74.15: Seeing that water streaming from the eyes, whose pupils were deep black and whose corners were red, Nala, stricken with grief, spoke these words.
t.3.74.16: That my kingdom was lost, I did not bring about myself; it was Kali who did that cowardly deed, and it was he, too, who caused me to abandon you.
t.3.74.18: That Kali dwelt within my body, burning because of your curse; constantly scorched by your curse, he remained there as though placed in a fire.
t.3.74.17: Yet long ago, while he dwelt in me, the foremost of those who uphold dharma, he was struck by your curse, uttered as you lived in the forest, distressed and grieving for me, who was left without a garment.
t.3.74.20: Having released me, that evil one departed, and then I came here for your sake, O broad-hipped one, for I have no other purpose.
t.3.74.19: And he has been conquered by my resolve and by my austerity; surely this must now be the end of our sorrow, O lovely one.
t.3.74.22: By the king's command, messengers are roaming the whole earth, proclaiming that Bhaimī, it is said, will choose a second husband.
t.3.74.21: How indeed could a woman ever abandon a husband who loves her and is devoted to her, and choose another, as you have done, timid one?
t.3.74.24: But Damayantī, having heard that lament of Nala, spoke these words, trembling and afraid, with her palms joined in reverence.
t.3.74.23: "Acting at her own will, she chooses as she pleases a man suited, as it were, to herself": the moment he heard this, Bhāṅgasvari came here in haste.
